title: Quadratic decision-tree bounds from block sensitivity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every integer \(n\ge1\), satisfies \[D(f)\le C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2?\] Here \(D(f)\) is deterministic worst-case bit-query complexity and \(\operatorname{bs}(f)\) is block sensitivity, with both measures defined below. The constant must be independent of \(n\) and of the function, and no logarithmic or dimension-dependent multiplier is allowed.
why: The two quantities measure different aspects of the information needed to determine a Boolean output: the worst adaptive query cost and the number of disjoint ways to change the output at one input. Their known cubic general upper bound and quadratic examples leave a basic gap. A uniform quadratic relation would sharpen the structure of query complexity across every total Boolean function.
status_note: The unrestricted inequality is posed in the checked Jukna draft and remains explicitly unresolved in the 2023 primary paper. The 2026 primary result checked here concerns block number and decision-tree size, not this general depth bound. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no resolution; this does not independently certify an exhaustive later literature review.

progress.text: Jukna records the universal \(D(f)=O(\operatorname{bs}(f)^2)\) question immediately after the cubic upper bound.
Chugh, Podder and Sanyal publish quadratic bounds for zebra functions and fixed-bounded-alternation functions, while explicitly retaining the general cubic-versus-quadratic gap.
Chakraborty and Gál post improved bounds on block number and decision-tree size. The main theorem and stated size consequences concern different measures from the proposed quadratic depth inequality.

sentences: The target is a universal quadratic upper bound on deterministic decision-tree depth in terms of block sensitivity.
A decision tree adaptively reads individual bits and must compute a total Boolean function correctly on every input.
Block sensitivity counts disjoint blocks whose separate flips all change the value at one common input.
The known general bound is cubic, while quadratic bounds hold for several restricted classes.
The proposed constant must work for every function and dimension, and recent results on tree size or counts of minimal blocks do not settle this depth question.

definitions: A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by an input coordinate \(i\in[n]\), with its two outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), the tree queries the bit \(x_i\) at the current node and follows the matching edge until it reaches a leaf. It computes \(f\) if the reached leaf equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Its worst-case query cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited on any input, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum such cost over all trees computing \(f\). Repeated coordinate queries are permitted and count again. A leaf-only tree has cost zero. The tree may be chosen separately for each known function, and its number of leaves or total nodes is not the measured resource. No efficient construction of the optimal tree from a truth table or circuit is required. For \(B\subseteq[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus B}\) denote the input obtained from \(x\) by flipping exactly the bits in \(B\). A nonempty block \(B\) is sensitive at \(x\) if \(f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus B})\). Define \(\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\) as the largest number \(t\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) that are each sensitive at this same input \(x\), and let \(\operatorname{bs}(f)=\max_x\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\). Each block is tested by flipping it alone from the common input, not by a cumulative sequence of flips. Blocks need not be singletons or have a specified size. This maximum disjoint collection is different from the number of all minimal sensitive blocks and from fractional block sensitivity. All total Boolean functions are included: monotonicity, symmetry, graph invariance, bounded alternation, balanced output and succinct circuit representation are not assumed. Constant functions have \(D(f)=\operatorname{bs}(f)=0\) and satisfy the proposed bound. Randomized and quantum queries are outside the definition of \(D(f)\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal quadratic inequality or of its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) that works for every dimension and every total function. A negative answer must establish that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a total nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) for which \(D(f)>C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\). Thus disproving the coefficient-one inequality is insufficient unless the ratios \(D(f)/\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\) are unbounded. A result for a subclass, a bound on decision-tree size instead of depth, or a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not meet the criterion. The smallest possible constant and an efficient tree-construction algorithm are not required.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s early draft poses \(D(f)=O(\operatorname{bs}(f)^2)\) as Research Problem 14.10 after Corollary 14.9 gives the general cubic upper bound. This card retains that constant-factor universal inequality, rather than asking only whether some polynomial relation exists.

Chugh, Podder and Sanyal’s 2023 paper states that the known general upper bound is cubic and the widest known separation is quadratic. Their Question 1 keeps the unrestricted gap open. Polynomial equivalence among measures, including the sensitivity theorem, does not by itself fix this exponent.

Their Theorem 4 establishes the quadratic bound for zebra functions, defined by having the same number of output changes along every increasing path from the all-zero input to the all-one input. This includes monotone and symmetric functions but is a restriction on the truth table. Their Theorem 5 also gives the quadratic bound when the maximum number of such changes is bounded by a fixed constant.

Chakraborty and Gál’s February 2026 paper improves bounds for the number of minimal sensitive blocks, and obtains consequences for the total size of decision trees. Those quantities differ from both the maximum number of disjoint sensitive blocks and the worst-case query depth in the present target. Its stated results do not establish the unrestricted quadratic inequality here.
